name: GTool: Graph Enhanced Tool Planning with Large Language Model
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.12725, cs.AI, submitted 18 Aug 2025). Also under OpenReview submission (forum id bn47cqGQ7l); peer-reviewed acceptance/venue not confirmed [uncertain].
authors_affiliation: Wenjie Chen, Wenbin Li, Di Yao (corresponding via submission), Xuying Meng, Chang Gong, Jingping Bi (corresponding author). Affiliations marked 1,2 for all authors; primary affiliation is the Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) [affiliation names inferred from author group, exact institution string not printed in HTML] [uncertain].
task_domain: tool-use (LLM tool planning: selecting, organizing, and sequencing tools/APIs to fulfill a user request)
problem_setting: Offline, single-agent, supervised tool planning. Given a tool set, historical user requests and their tool trajectories, the method first induces a tool-dependency graph, then for each new request generates a tool-invocation sequence. A complete tool-dependency graph is NOT assumed available; dependencies are induced from historical trajectories and are typically incomplete. Training is supervised (instruction tuning of a GNN encoder with the LLM frozen); inference performs one-shot planning with a single LLM interaction per request. Supervision is available (ground-truth tool trajectories used as labels).
what_is_retrieved: tools (a request-specific subgraph of candidate tools and their inter-tool dependencies), encoded into a single <graph token> rather than text passages.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external store: a tool-dependency graph built offline from a fixed tool set and historical tool trajectories. The graph is not written/grown during deployment; for each request a request-specific subgraph is derived from this static graph.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Recovery of the complete minimal needed set: the objective is to produce the full correct multi-tool dependency-correct plan (sequence) for a request, evaluated by Node-F1 (right tool set), Link-F1 (right dependency topology) and NED (right ordering), rather than a fixed top-k ranking. Naive baselines (BM25/COLT/Graph RAG-Tool Fusion) use top-k retrieval (top-5 / top-3) but GTool itself targets variable-size dependency-complete plans.
retrieval_unit: tool-API node and KG-subgraph: each node is a tool (with a BERT-embedded document attribute) and directed edges are inter-tool dependencies; the retrieved/used unit is a request-specific tool dependency subgraph compressed into one graph-level representation (<graph token>).
index_source: Static corpus, offline-induced. The tool graph G={V,E} is constructed once from the tool set T and historical trajectories H (edges added between consecutive tools in each trajectory). It is not grown at test time.
index_structure_topology: Dependency GRAPH: a directed tool-dependency graph (node=tool, edge=output-of-A-is-precondition-for-B). For each request a request-specific graph G(q) is formed by adding a super node for the request connected to all tool nodes.
retriever_type: Learned generative graph encoder: a GNN-based encoder (TransformerConv, 3 layers) maps the request-specific tool graph to a graph-level embedding (graph-as-token), aligned with the LLM. Not BM25/dense-text retrieval; the dependency-aware selection is done by the GNN-to-LLM pipeline (BM25/COLT are baselines only).
retriever_learning_signal: Downstream-task-effectiveness plus an auxiliary self-supervised signal: the GNN encoder parameters are trained jointly by (a) the tool-planning autoregressive loss L_TL = p_M(tau_G | w) (supervised on ground-truth trajectories) and (b) a missing-dependency edge-prediction loss L_MDPL (autoregressive yes/no edge existence), combined as L = L_TL + lambda * L_MDPL (lambda=0.1). The LLM is frozen; only the GNN encoder is optimized.
query_construction: Intent/request node: the raw user request q is embedded by a language model f (BERT) and added as a request-specific super node v_{n+1} with directed edges from all tool nodes to it; the request node's GNN representation h_{n+1}=h_G serves as the query-conditioned graph summary. The textual prompt also lists tool names and the request.
query_granularity: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single request-specific graph and one <graph token> are constructed per user request before planning.
when_to_retrieve: one-shot: the request-specific tool graph is constructed and the graph token produced once per request, then a single LLM call generates the full plan. (GTool interacts with the LLM only once per request.)
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule (always-on, once per request): graph construction and graph-token generation happen unconditionally for every request before the single planning call; there is no confidence/uncertainty/router trigger.
reranking: No explicit reranking stage. Relevance is handled implicitly by the request-specific super node which lets request-relevant tool/dependency information propagate to the graph token; baselines (BM25/COLT) use similarity sorting but GTool does not apply a separate reranker.
retrieved_context_refinement: Graph-level compression/distillation: instead of injecting tool descriptions and dependencies as text, GTool distills the entire request-specific dependency subgraph into a single graph-level embedding (<graph token>), reducing irrelevant-tool influence and per-request tokens by over 80-95%. The MDPL task also refines the graph by predicting/imputing masked (missing) edges.
how_retrieved_used: latent-token injection: the graph representation h_G is injected into the LLM prompt as a special <graph_embed> token (bounded by [/graph]) alongside tool names and the request; the LLM reasons over this latent graph token to autoregressively generate the tool trajectory. (Prompt augmentation via a soft/latent token, not text.)
planning_integration: retrieve-then-plan, one-shot: build request-specific tool graph -> encode to graph token -> single LLM call generates the full tool-invocation sequence. No tree search, no per-step interleaving, no MCTS; planning is a single autoregressive generation conditioned on the graph token.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-answer: the full plan (entire tool trajectory) is produced in one LLM pass with one injected graph token; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-tool-call.
retrieved_item_representation: latent-soft token: the injected item is a single learned graph-level embedding (<graph token>) representing the request-specific tool dependency subgraph, not raw text/trajectory/program.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Distilled structural summary: a graph-level latent representation aggregating request-specific tool semantics and inter-tool dependency topology (above raw per-tool docstrings, abstracting the dependency subgraph).
noise_robustness_mechanism: Missing-dependency prediction with LLMs (MDPL): edges are randomly masked with probability rho during training and the model is trained to predict masked/absent edges (balanced positive/negative sampling, size alpha), explicitly modeling edge incompleteness so the graph token stays reliable under incomplete/sparse dependencies. The request-specific super node also suppresses irrelevant-tool noise. Robust down to 90% missing edges in most settings.
memory_type: graph (a static tool-dependency graph). No episodic/skill/workflow memory; the graph is induced offline and frozen.
write_back: false. No new experiences/cases/trajectories are written back to a memory at inference time; only the offline-induced tool graph is used (graph construction is a one-time preprocessing step, not online write-back).
online_growth: No. The tool-dependency store is frozen after offline induction from historical trajectories; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
write_back_trigger: never: there is no write-back mechanism; the tool graph is built once offline from historical trajectories and the GNN encoder is trained, after which inference adds nothing to the store.
failure_experience_usage: Not used as stored experiences. There is no success/failure experience memory. (The closest analogue is MDPL's negative edge candidates (l='no') used contrastively during edge-prediction training, but these are graph-structure negatives, not failed-trajectory experiences.)
memory_evolution_update: append-only / static: edges are added once from trajectories during construction (E <- E ∪ consecutive-tool edges); after offline induction the graph is not mutated, merged, pruned, or refined at deployment. MDPL imputes missing edges only implicitly via the trained encoder, not by editing the stored graph.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partially: tool selection is driven by a learned (trained) GNN encoder aligned to the LLM rather than a fixed similarity top-k, but it is NOT an RL/MDP-optimized retrieval policy. Training uses supervised planning loss plus a self-supervised edge-prediction loss (no RL, no Q-learning).
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent, single private tool graph per dataset; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing. (The GNN module is backbone-agnostic and can be paired with various LLMs, but memory is not shared across agents.)
benchmarks: TaskBench (three sub-datasets: HuggingFace, Daily Life, Multimedia), ToolE (MetaTool), and ToolBench (large-scale, >16,000 RESTful APIs; I2/I3 scenarios used).
benchmark_family: tool (tool planning / tool selection): TaskBench and ToolE are tool-planning benchmarks; ToolBench (>16k RESTful APIs) is the large-scale tool benchmark.
baselines: Naive: BM25, COLT, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (GRTF). Tuning-free: HuggingGPT, TaskBench. Tuning-based: GNN4Plan, ToolNet, Tool-Planner. (Backbones: LLaMA-2-7B, Vicuna-13B, Qwen3-14B in main table; plus 7 more backbones in appendix. Methods needing multiple LLM interactions e.g. STE, Toolink, ToolLLaMA are excluded.)
key_metrics: Node F1-Score (n-F1, correct tool selection, higher better), Link F1-Score (l-F1, dependency-topology preservation, higher better), Normalized Edit Distance (NED, invocation-order correctness, lower better); plus Time/Request (seconds) and per-request token consumption for efficiency.
headline_result: Over 29.6% performance improvement over SOTA baselines with a light-weight 7B LLM backbone (LLaMA-2-7B). E.g. on HuggingFace/LLaMA-2-7B GTool reaches n-F1=0.7913, l-F1=0.5403, NED=0.2537 vs best baseline GNN4Plan n-F1=0.4853; paper also cites 27.9% n-F1 growth over GNN4Plan. On ToolBench (Qwen3-14B) n-F1=0.6126, l-F1=0.3018 with Time/R=2.02s (~1/10 of baselines).
ablations: Four ablations (Table 3): w/o RS (remove request-specific super node, use average pooling), w/o MDPL (remove missing-dependency prediction), w/o Both (remove both but still train for graph token), w/o All (no graph at all, prompt with tool names + brief instruction only). On LLaMA-2-7B: removing RS node drops n-F1 by 9.92%, l-F1 by 17.9%, NED by 22.5%; removing MDPL drops n-F1 3.32%, l-F1 3.83%; w/o Both drops n-F1 22.5%, l-F1 35.7%, NED +60.5%; w/o All collapses (n-F1=0.1566). RS node is the dominant component; effects are larger on weaker backbones (LLaMA-2-7B > Vicuna-13B). Hyperparameter analysis: alpha=4, lambda=0.1, n_l=3 optimal.
evaluation_decoupling: Partially. End-to-end planning is reported with n-F1/l-F1/NED (l-F1 captures dependency-topology recovery, a structural/intrinsic-like signal). A separate intrinsic 'accuracy of missing dependency prediction' is reported in Appendix B.3, decoupling the MDPL edge-prediction quality from final planning. Classic Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics are not the headline.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both: outcome is tool selection (n-F1); process/structure quality is also scored via l-F1 (preserves dependency-graph topology) and NED (correctness of invocation order), plus appendix MDPL edge-prediction accuracy and case studies.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Strong efficiency gains: GTool needs only one LLM interaction per request; reduces per-request tokens by over 80% vs HuggingGPT/TaskBench (paper also states >95% pre-task token reduction vs prompt-encoding methods); inference time ~1/10 of SOTA baselines. On ToolBench, Time/R=2.02s vs HuggingGPT 12.77s, Tool-Planner 6.67s, TaskBench 47.24s, GNN4Plan 47.58s. Training cost: ~200 GPU-hours total on 2x NVIDIA A100-80G.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Budget-capped / compressed: tool descriptions are NOT placed in the prompt; instead the entire request-specific dependency subgraph is compressed into one <graph token>, so the prompt holds only tool names + brief instruction + the graph token, achieving >80-95% token reduction. No fixed top-k injected items; the graph token summarizes the request-relevant subgraph. (Naive baselines used top-5/top-3.)
builds_on: GNN-to-LLM graph-as-token alignment (e.g. GraphGPT-style 'graph as sequence/token', GNN adapters for LLMs), TransformerConv (Shi et al. 2020) as the GNN encoder, BERT for node/request text embeddings, link-prediction / graph autoencoder ideas (Kipf & Welling; Zhang & Chen) for missing-edge prediction, and supervised instruction tuning for LLM tool planning (TaskBench, HuggingGPT).
contrasts_with: Tuning-free prompt-based planners (HuggingGPT, TaskBench, ControlLLM, ART, ToolFormer) that encode tools/dependencies as long text; graph-traversal retrieval (Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, ToolNet) and clustering (Tool-Planner) that assume complete dependency structures and/or need multiple LLM calls; tuning-based GNN4Plan (requires extra inference to generate textual steps and assumes complete graphs). GTool is positioned as the first to model INCOMPLETE tool dependencies, freeze the LLM, and plan in a single LLM call.
lineage: Sub-topic E (tool-use): retrieval/graph-augmented LLM tool planning. Within the tool-retrieval lineage that moved from flat text retrieval -> dependency/knowledge-graph-aware tool retrieval (COLT, ToolNet, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, GNN4Plan); GTool advances this by compressing a request-specific dependency subgraph into a latent graph token and explicitly handling incomplete dependencies via missing-edge prediction.
code_url: N/A (no official code repository found as of search; not linked from the arXiv page or paper). [uncertain]
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle over cases).
explicit_cbr_grounding: false. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is graph-augmented tool planning.
tool_document_engineering: Tool documents d(t) are embedded with a language model f (BERT) and used as node attributes a_i = f(d(t_i)); the request is embedded as the super-node attribute. Descriptions are thus encoded into graph node features (not raw docstrings in the prompt, no synthetic-query augmentation). This is graph-feature engineering rather than text expansion.
index_content_separation: Yes (effectively): heavy tool descriptions are encoded into the graph/node features and compressed into a single graph token, while the LLM prompt carries only lightweight tool names + instruction + the graph token, separating a lightweight injected representation from the heavy content (>80-95% token savings).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static tool index (graph built once offline from historical trajectories; not live-synchronized). Integration protocol: tools are APIs/RESTful APIs (ToolBench uses >16k RESTful APIs); no MCP / live CRUD auto-sync. Planning produces a tool sequence consumed via function/tool-calling conceptually but the paper does not implement a live tool-sync protocol.
tool_dependency_awareness: Yes — this is the core contribution. Retrieval/selection explicitly models inter-tool dependencies as a directed dependency graph (output-of-A is precondition for B), with a request-specific super node and a missing-dependency prediction task (MDPL) to handle incomplete dependency edges; the GNN encoder is dependency-aware and the graph token conveys dependency topology to the LLM.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not CBR; no case adaptation/revision step).
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (primary research paper, not a survey).
benchmark_construction_and_size: Not a benchmark paper. Datasets used (Table 4 statistics): HuggingFace (23 tools, 225 edges, 2178/726/726 train/val/test), Multimedia (40 tools, 449 edges, 1788/596/597), Daily Life (40 tools, 1560 edges, 1672/57/558), ToolE (15 tools, 154 edges, 298/99/100); plus ToolBench (>16,000 RESTful APIs, I2/I3 scenarios, invocation chains generated by ChatGPT). Tool graphs are constructed from historical/invocation trajectories (consecutive-tool edges); answer verifiability via ground-truth trajectories (n-F1/l-F1/NED).
